Right now I'm working for a company that builds them - They're Delta-style configurations though, and those come with their own set of frustrations so I suggest getting a cartesian first. (like the one pictured.) - Cartesians are machines that move on 1 axis per motor. Motor 1 does X, Motor 2 does Y, Motor 3 (sometimes also 4) do Z. They're much more positionally accurate and a hell of a lot less fiddly. Honestly, the Ender 3 is a great starter machine. CR-10 are solid too.

As you can see, the ones I'm designing are using T-slot (technically V-slot from OpenBuilds) and Delrin Rollers. These are cheap, they're accurate, and they're quiet. Most of the open source software used with them is pretty damn good these days, and you generally only need to know a handful of things about your machine to use them. Important things to know about a 3D printer: Nozzle size, Printable Area, Filament size, and...generally that's it.

Something I've always been curious about, could you use a delta style rig to make a 5 axis device? It looks like you should be able to, but maybe they don't work like that.

The problem with anything more than a 3-axis device, is that once you rotate the toolhead, the computational model for calculating toolhead positions gains an extra dimension of complexity. This is why at most we have 5-continual axis in commercial machines. It gets too complex @ 6 axis to determine where a tool will fit computationally. It might be intuitive to us, but mathematically it's not.

Deltas can actually rotate the end effector if you disjoint the arms on it. Normal deltas, you'll notice have 6 arms. 3 in parallel sets. Those sets are there to actually provide a rotational axis worth of constraint. Separate their joints (so that they move independently) and yes - a delta can be made to rotate on the ABC axis'
